title: Chemical digestion, enzymes and absorption
blurb: Match each nutrient to where its digestion starts, the enzymes that split it, its end products and where they are absorbed.
question: Carlos eats a turkey sandwich with butter. Where does digestion of each nutrient begin, which enzymes finish the job, and why does the fat take a different route into the body?

teach.h: Breaking big molecules into small ones
teach.body: Formally, chemical digestion is the enzyme-driven hydrolysis of large food molecules (polymers) into small units (monomers) that can be absorbed. In plain English: chewing and churning make pieces smaller, but only enzymes cut the chemical bonds. Each enzyme fits one kind of molecule, its substrate, and its name usually ends in -ase and hints at that substrate: lipase for lipids, lactase for lactose.

teach.h: The three big nutrients side by side
teach.caption: Nucleic acids are split by pancreatic nucleases into nucleotides, then sugars, bases and phosphate, absorbed into blood.

steps.label: Blood capillaries
steps.sub: Then the hepatic portal vein to the liver

teach.caption: Sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = glucose + galactose; maltose = glucose + glucose. Humans cannot digest cellulose (fiber).

steps.label: Stomach
steps.sub: HCl activates pepsinogen to pepsin (works near pH 2)

steps.label: Duodenum
steps.sub: Trypsin and chymotrypsin (trypsin works near pH 8)

teach.caption: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed along with dietary fat.

teach.h: Why the small intestine does most of the work
teach.body: Most chemical digestion and most absorption happen in the small intestine. Pancreatic enzymes and bile arrive in the duodenum, and brush-border enzymes sit on the microvilli. Circular folds, villi and microvilli give a huge surface. Each villus contains blood capillaries (for monosaccharides and amino acids) and a central lacteal (for fats). Each enzyme also has an optimum pH, which is why bicarbonate must neutralize acid chyme before pancreatic enzymes can work.

teach.caption: Note how much of the abdomen the small intestine fills: its great length gives it the surface area to absorb most nutrients.

head: Region
Absorbs
rows: Vitamin B12 (needs intrinsic factor), bile salts
Water and electrolytes; bacterial vitamin K

teach.body: Carlos chews his sandwich and salivary amylase starts on the bread's starch. In his stomach, pepsin begins on the turkey's protein. In the duodenum, bicarbonate neutralizes the chyme; pancreatic amylase, trypsin and chymotrypsin continue, and bile salts emulsify the butter so lipase can split it. Brush-border enzymes finish sugars and peptides. Glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries; the fat's products leave as chylomicrons through the lacteals.

teach.text: Carbohydrate digestion starts in the MOUTH, protein digestion in the STOMACH. Bile is not an enzyme: it emulsifies, lipase digests. Fat products enter LACTEALS (lymph), not blood capillaries.

items: Carbohydrates: amylases and brush-border enzymes to monosaccharides; absorbed into blood.
Proteins: pepsin, then trypsin and chymotrypsin, then peptidases to amino acids; into blood.
Fats: bile emulsifies, lipase digests to fatty acids and monoglycerides; into lacteals as chylomicrons.
Most digestion and absorption: small intestine (villi, microvilli, brush-border enzymes).
Ileum absorbs B12 and bile salts; large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes.

summary: You can now say where digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats begins, name the enzymes that act on each and their end products, and state where those products are absorbed. You can also explain why fats travel through lacteals while sugars and amino acids enter blood capillaries.

A.q: In which organ does the chemical digestion of protein begin?
A.why: Chief cells release pepsinogen, which stomach acid converts to pepsin, the first protein-digesting enzyme.

whyNot.0: The mouth begins carbohydrate digestion (salivary amylase), not protein digestion.
whyNot.2: Trypsin and chymotrypsin continue protein digestion in the duodenum, but pepsin has already started it.
whyNot.3: The jejunum is mainly a site of absorption; protein digestion began two regions earlier.

A.q: Into which structures are the end products of fat digestion absorbed?
A.why: Fatty acids and monoglycerides are packaged into chylomicrons and enter the lacteals, the lymph vessels in each villus.

whyNot.0: Blood capillaries take up monosaccharides and amino acids; fat products leave as chylomicrons through lacteals.
whyNot.1: The colon absorbs water and electrolytes, not the products of fat digestion.
whyNot.3: The hepatic portal vein carries absorbed sugars and amino acids, not chylomicrons.

A.q: Which enzyme is correctly paired with its substrate?
A.why: Lipase digests fats (triglycerides) into fatty acids and monoglycerides.

whyNot.0: Lactase digests lactose; sucrose is digested by sucrase.
whyNot.1: Pepsin digests protein; starch is digested by amylase.
whyNot.2: Trypsin digests protein; nucleic acids are digested by nucleases.

B.q: Which carbohydrate cannot be digested by human enzymes?
B.why: Humans lack an enzyme for cellulose, so it passes through as dietary fiber, which gut bacteria ferment.

whyNot.1: Plant starch is digested by salivary and pancreatic amylase.
whyNot.2: Glycogen is an animal storage carbohydrate that amylase can break down.
whyNot.3: Lactose is digested by the brush-border enzyme lactase.

B.q: Which statement about nutrient absorption is CORRECT?
options: Fatty acids enter blood capillaries in the villi
Most amino acids are absorbed across the stomach wall
Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine
The large intestine absorbs most of the glucose
B.why: Villi, microvilli and brush-border enzymes make the small intestine the site of most absorption.

whyNot.0: Fat products enter the lacteals (lymph) as chylomicrons, not blood capillaries.
whyNot.1: The stomach absorbs little (some water, alcohol, aspirin); amino acids are absorbed in the small intestine.
whyNot.3: Glucose is absorbed in the small intestine; the large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes.

B.q: Pepsin stops working soon after chyme enters the duodenum. What is the best explanation?
options: Bile salts coat it and block its active site
Bicarbonate raises the pH above its optimum
It is absorbed into lacteals with the fats
Its substrate, starch, has all been digested
B.why: Pepsin works best near pH 2. Pancreatic bicarbonate neutralizes the chyme, so the pH rises far above pepsin's optimum.

whyNot.0: Bile salts emulsify fat; they do not inhibit pepsin.
whyNot.2: Lacteals absorb chylomicrons from fat digestion, not enzymes.
whyNot.3: Pepsin's substrate is protein, not starch.

C.q: Carlos eats a sandwich of bread, turkey and butter. Which statement correctly traces one of its nutrients?
options: Turkey protein ends as amino acids in blood capillaries
Bread starch begins digestion in the stomach with pepsin
Butter fat is split into fatty acids by bile in the duodenum
Bread starch ends as glucose carried away in lacteals
C.why: Protein is digested to amino acids, which are absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi.

whyNot.1: Starch digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase; pepsin digests protein.
whyNot.2: Bile only emulsifies fat; pancreatic lipase splits it into fatty acids and monoglycerides.
whyNot.3: Glucose enters blood capillaries; lacteals carry the products of fat digestion.

C.q: A medication blocks pancreatic lipase. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Bile can no longer emulsify dietary fat
Starch digestion halts in the duodenum
Pepsin can no longer digest protein
Less fat is broken into fatty acids
C.why: Lipase is the enzyme that splits fat into fatty acids and monoglycerides, so blocking it leaves more fat undigested.

whyNot.0: Bile's emulsifying action is physical and does not depend on lipase.
whyNot.1: Starch is digested by amylase, which the drug does not affect.
whyNot.2: Pepsin is a stomach enzyme independent of pancreatic lipase.

C.q: Which sequence lists, in order, the enzymes that act on starch from the mouth to the brush border?
C.why: Salivary amylase starts in the mouth, pancreatic amylase continues in the duodenum, and maltase on the brush border splits maltose into glucose.

whyNot.0: Salivary amylase acts first, in the mouth, before pancreatic amylase.
whyNot.1: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach and plays no part in starch digestion.
whyNot.3: Lipase digests fat, and lactase acts on lactose (milk sugar), not on starch fragments.

reteach.title: Taking apart a model built from bricks
reteach.question: Imagine trying to push a large brick model through a mail slot. What has to happen to it, and who does the dismantling?

blocks.h: Only single bricks fit through the slot
blocks.body: Starch, protein and fat are big built models. The wall of the small intestine is the mail slot: only single bricks fit through. Enzymes are specialist tools, each able to undo one kind of joint, so amylase works on starch but not protein. Bile is the helper who breaks a greasy lump into small pieces so the lipase tool can reach every joint. Sugar and amino-acid bricks drop into the blood; fat bricks take the lymph route through lacteals.

blocks.text: The helper is not a tool: bile has no enzyme. And the fat bricks use a different door: lacteals, not blood capillaries.

explain.body: Salivary amylase starts on starch in the mouth; pancreatic amylase continues in the duodenum. Brush-border maltase, sucrase and lactase split disaccharides into monosaccharides, which enter blood capillaries and travel in the hepatic portal vein to the liver.

test.q: Lactase splits lactose into which two monosaccharides?
test.why: Lactose is glucose + galactose, so lactase releases those two monosaccharides.

whyNot.0: Glucose and fructose are the products of sucrose, split by sucrase.
whyNot.2: Two glucose molecules come from maltose, split by maltase.
whyNot.3: No common dietary disaccharide is made of galactose and fructose.

explain.body: Pepsin (activated by stomach acid, optimum near pH 2) begins protein digestion. In the duodenum, trypsin and chymotrypsin (optimum near pH 8) continue it, and brush-border peptidases finish it. Amino acids enter blood capillaries.

test.q: Which enzyme continues protein digestion in the small intestine?
test.why: Trypsin (from pancreatic trypsinogen) continues protein digestion in the duodenum, where the pH suits it.

whyNot.0: Pepsin begins protein digestion in the stomach and stops working once the chyme is neutralized.

explain.body: Fat digestion happens mostly in the small intestine. Bile salts emulsify fat into droplets; pancreatic lipase splits them into fatty acids and monoglycerides. Intestinal cells package these into chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals.

test.q: What are the end products of fat digestion?
test.why: Pancreatic lipase splits triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides.

whyNot.0: Amino acids and dipeptides come from protein digestion.
whyNot.1: Glucose and galactose come from lactose digestion.
whyNot.2: Emulsified droplets are fat that has been broken up by bile but not yet chemically digested.

explain.body: The stomach absorbs little. The jejunum absorbs most nutrients. The ileum absorbs vitamin B12 (which needs intrinsic factor from parietal cells) and bile salts. The large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes and gains vitamin K from its bacteria.

test.q: Which vitamin is absorbed in the ileum with the help of intrinsic factor?
test.why: Intrinsic factor from the stomach's parietal cells binds vitamin B12 so it can be absorbed in the ileum.

whyNot.1: Vitamin K is made by bacteria in the large intestine.
whyNot.2: Vitamin D is fat-soluble and is absorbed with dietary fat, without intrinsic factor.
whyNot.3: Vitamins A and E are fat-soluble and are absorbed with dietary fat, without intrinsic factor.
